how_it_wins:
Cast a Vampire and Edgar mints a 1/1 from the command zone. That is the whole ignition. It costs nothing and works with Edgar never cast (stacks 002, 010). A castable Vampire is drawn in 95.0% of games at mean turn 2.22.

The bodies are not the kill. Forge on v1.0.0, 400 games: combat damage to players mean 29.07, median 13.0, and a go-wide refactor that cut the lords fell to 18.20 and won 31/400 beside 50/400. Eight sacrifice outlets by role, six needing neither mana nor a tap, feed ten death payoffs. A death becomes a card (Crossway Troublemakers, Skullclamp, Liliana), a counter on every Vampire (Cordial Vampire), two on the equipped one (Blade of the Bloodchief), or a point off each opponent (Cruel Celebrant). Elenda is the hinge: she grows on every death and dies into X lifelink Vampires under the doublers; that count needs a stack scenario.

What has to be true: an outlet and a payoff on the battlefield together. The free outlet is drawn in 72.3% of games, the death-drain pair in 37.2%, and nothing measures the pair. Read the board, not the rate. Mana is the constraint the model does see: a turn-2 stall in 24.6% of games, mana-short in 4,439 of 5,318 stall turns.

Two verified closes need no combat damage. Stack 003: seven attacking Vampires under Sanctum Seeker and Bloodletter of Aclazotz take 14 off each seat on attack declaration, before blockers. Stacks 004 and 006: Bloodthirsty Conqueror with Vito or Sanguine Bond is a deterministic table kill from any lifegain. Each rests on one card: Bloodletter 4.1% assembled, Conqueror 7.8%; Vampiric Tutor makes it 9.4% and 15.1%.

The table misreads this as an aggro deck and wipes it. With a payoff out, the wipe is your drain: log 002, eleven deaths, 11 off every opponent. Five logged games, five losses, none on the board: counters, running dry, a tutored infinite, Purphoros pings. None yet on v1.1.1.

combo_lines.002: This line turns on one question: does Edgar's eminence work while he sits in the command zone, never cast? It does. The trigger's intervening 'if' is checked again on resolution and the ability names the zone it works from. Everything else is one token event replaced twice. Anointed Procession and Mondrak, Glory Dominus each get one application, you choose the order, and 1 becomes 4 either way. Vampire Socialite's 'enters with' clause puts a counter on every token and on the Aetherborn because an opponent lost life earlier in the turn: cast the Vampire after the turn's first drain, not before. What it proves: five bodies, four of them 2/2s, for {B}{B}, commander untouched. What it does not prove: the tokens are created, not cast, so they never re-trigger eminence; and Cordial Vampire never fires here because nothing dies. The mint alone is not the engine. The mint plus an outlet is.
combo_lines.003: The line turns on Bloodletter of Aclazotz being a replacement effect that applies once per life-loss event, on your turn. Seven attacking Vampires give seven Sanctum Seeker triggers; each opponent's 1 becomes 2; seven events is 14 per seat. Your gain is not doubled, because Bloodletter replaces opponents' loss only, so you gain 7. The seat at 14 hits 0 on the seventh trigger and leaves on the state-based check before blockers are declared; the seat at 21 is at 7 with 20 power still attacking. Put Edgar's counter trigger on top; it changes nothing about the drain. What it proves: with Bloodletter and Seeker out, attackers times two per opponent is the drain before combat. What it does not prove: the pairing is drawn in 4.1% of games (9.4% with Vampiric Tutor) at mean turn 6.71, so it is a windfall, not the plan. Four of the seven attackers are eminence tokens. They attack; they do not need to connect.
combo_lines.004: The line turns on Bloodthirsty Conqueror's trigger reading 'loses life', not 'is dealt damage'. Vito's drain is life loss, the parenthetical is reminder text, and the loop runs: Vito drains 3, Conqueror gains 3, Vito triggers again with a fresh target. Thirteen Vito resolutions kill 9 and 30 from a 3-life seed, and the killing loss still triggers Conqueror, so an opponent leaving mid-loop does not stop it. What it proves: a deterministic, shortcut-legal table kill from any lifegain at all. A Cruel Celebrant trigger, a lifelink hit, Elenda's tokens connecting. What it does not prove: safety. Conqueror is a creature and every iteration passes priority, so one instant-speed removal spell on either half ends it; the stack assumes no opponent holds one. Drawn in 7.8% of games, 15.1% with the tutor. The pilot has said the infinite is out of the plan. The 99 still holds it, and with both pieces out the next lifegain is the loop whether you intended it or not. That case needs a stack scenario.
combo_lines.006: Same loop, enchantment half. Sanguine Bond's text is Vito's word for word, so the line turns on the same reading of Conqueror's trigger. The differences are arithmetic and exposure. Three does not divide 11 or 26, so each kill overkills by 1: count iterations up, never assume exact zeros. Bond is an enchantment, so the loop has one creature half instead of two. Conqueror is the only target for instant-speed creature removal, and the Bond needs a Despark, an Anguished Unmaking or a Stroke of Midnight. What it proves: the deck's second contained infinite, verified on its own, at zero additional mana. What it does not prove: redundancy. Both loops share Conqueror, which is why deck-audit prices him as a single point of failure rather than counting two routes. Bond costs five and does nothing alone; Vito costs three and grants lifelink for {3}{B}{B}. Given the choice, Vito first.
combo_lines.010: The line turns on whether Elspeth, Storm Slayer's replacement effect sees a token made by a trigger from the command zone. It does: the effect keys on tokens being created under your control, and you control the eminence trigger even though Edgar has never been on the battlefield. Three doublers, one application each, 1 to 8 in all six orders; you choose the order and it does not matter. Anointed Procession's 'an effect would create' wording is inert here, since the rule written for that template applies whether it is chosen first or after another doubler. What it proves: on this board every Vampire spell is nine bodies for its mana cost. What it does not prove: Vampire Socialite and Cordial Vampire were kept off this board on purpose, so stack 002's counter math is not composed here; and Elspeth is a planeswalker who was targeted at once in log 001 and lost to an all-in swing in log 005. Eight tokens are eight things to convert, not eight damage.

card_roles.Edgar Markov: Your engine never leaves the command zone: every Vampire spell you cast mints a token, and stack 002 shows two doublers turning one mint into four bodies. Cast him late as a finisher — his attack trigger pumps the army you already built.
card_roles.Anointed Procession: Doubles every token event you own, eminence mints included. Land it before the big turn, not after — stack 009's exact-lethal line runs through it.
card_roles.Mondrak, Glory Dominus: Doubler number two, on a body that can buy indestructible. Stacked with Procession, one cast makes four tokens — the order is yours and the math is the same (stack 002).
card_roles.Elspeth, Storm Slayer: Doubler number three, plus her own Soldiers, a team-wide flying turn, and a -3 that answers a resolved threat. Protect her loyalty with your width.
card_roles.Ocelot Pride: One mana that turns any lifegain turn into an end-step token — and with the city's blessing it copies every token that entered this turn. Play it early; it gets silly late.
card_roles.Purphoros, God of the Forge: Two damage to each opponent per arriving body — stack 008 prices one two-mana Vampire at 10 per opponent through the doublers. He's usually not a creature, so sweepers miss him.
card_roles.Impact Tremors: Your cheapest converter. Turn-2 Tremors means every body for the rest of the game pings the whole table — untick nothing, just cast Vampires into it.
card_roles.Warleader's Call: Converter and anthem in one: the damage half kills without combat, the +1/+1 half makes the combat kill real. Stack 009 shows it composing with Tremors and Purphoros.
card_roles.Corpse Knight: Converter number four, as life loss rather than damage — and it hits each opponent. A Vampire body that makes every other body hurt.
card_roles.Witty Roastmaster: Converter number five. Redundancy IS the plan here: you see one of these effects by turn 6 in 62.6% of games because the deck runs five of them.
card_roles.Blood Artist: Every creature death — yours included — drains. He hits one player per death, so aim him; his real job is making the table's board wipe pay you.
card_roles.Cruel Celebrant: The wide death drain: each opponent loses 1 per death of yours. When a wipe is on the stack, count your creatures — that's damage the table eats for killing your board.
card_roles.Legion's Landing // Adanto, the First Fo: One mana for a lifelink body, then a land that mints one every turn. Transform it the turn you attack with three — it fixes white forever after.
card_roles.Mavren Fein, Dusk Apostle: Attack with one nontoken Vampire and he pays you a token — doubled by your multipliers. Free width every single combat.
card_roles.Bloodline Keeper // Lord of Lineage: A token engine every turn, and a +2/+2 lord once you have five Vampires. The flip costs {B} — plan a real black source, because Cavern of Souls' mana can't pay an activation.
card_roles.Charismatic Conqueror: Taxes everything your opponents deploy untapped: they tap it down or you get a lifelink Vampire. Either way you're not the one paying.
card_roles.Preacher of the Schism: Point him at the biggest life total and he mints a body; attack while you're ahead and he draws you cards. Attack whoever you'd attack anyway — he pays either way.
card_roles.Vampire Socialite: Somebody loses life almost every turn you take, so your Vampires enter with an extra counter — stack 002's tokens arrived as 2/2s. Menace makes her a fine early attacker too.
card_roles.Cordial Vampire: Every creature death, anywhere at the table, grows your whole tribe. Between your drains and Skullclamp, deaths are something you manufacture.
card_roles.Drana, Liberator of Malakir: First-strike flier who counters up every attacker before regular damage lands. Swing her early — the counters compound.
card_roles.Knight of the Ebon Legion: A one-drop that scales: someone loses 4 life most turns in this deck, and the pump ability makes him a real late threat on an empty draw.
card_roles.Vampire of the Dire Moon: Deathtouch plus lifelink for one mana — the best blocker rate in the 99, and every lifelink hit is trigger fuel for Vito.
card_roles.Indulgent Aristocrat: One-drop lifelinker carrying the deck's sac outlet: two mana turns a doomed token into a counter on every Vampire. Sacrifice in response to exile removal and get paid.
card_roles.Voldaren Epicure: One red mana: a body, a ping to each opponent, and a Blood token that loots away a flooded land later. Everything this deck wants, in miniature.
card_roles.Vampire Cutthroat: Skulk means he connects turn after turn, and every hit is lifegain — which Vito and Sanguine Bond turn into somebody else's problem.
card_roles.Champion of Dusk: Your biggest refill: draw a card per Vampire you control, life is the fee. Cast him after the swarm, not before — five bodies means five cards.
card_roles.Sanctum Seeker: Every attacking Vampire drains the whole table — stack 003 prices seven attackers at 14 life per opponent under Bloodletter. Protect him on the big swing; he's the combat kill's engine.
card_roles.Bloodletter of Aclazotz: Doubles opponents' life loss on your turn — combat, converters, drains, all of it (stacks 003 and 007). The triple-black cost is the hardest cast in the deck; sequence your black sources for him.
card_roles.Bloodthirsty Conqueror: The infinite's spine: with Vito or Sanguine Bond down, any lifegain ends the table (stacks 004 and 006). Alone he's still a 5/5 flying deathtouch that pays you for every point anyone loses.
card_roles.Vito, Thorn of the Dusk Rose: Every point you gain, a target opponent loses. Verified kill loop with Conqueror (stack 004); honest drain engine with any lifelinker; his activation can grant the team lifelink for the alpha strike.
card_roles.Sanguine Bond: Vito's text on an enchantment — harder to remove, same verified loop with Conqueror (stack 006). Redundancy for the found-money kill.
card_roles.Throne of the God-Pharaoh: End-step drain equal to your tapped creatures — a second combat's worth of loss after a wide attack, doubled under Bloodletter (stack 007). Only tapped bodies count, so attack first, then collect.
card_roles.Legion Lieutenant: A two-mana lord. Nothing clever — every token gets bigger, and you make a lot of tokens.
card_roles.Stromkirk Captain: Lord plus first strike for the whole tribe, which makes blocking your swarm a losing trade every time.
card_roles.Captivating Vampire: Lord with a theft engine: tap five untapped Vampires to steal the best creature on the table, permanently. Steal before you attack — the ability needs untapped bodies.
card_roles.Patchwork Banner: Anthem and fixer in one: +1/+1 for the tribe and a rock that makes any colour. Name Vampire and never look back.
card_roles.Shared Animosity: Attack with six Vampires and each gets +5/+0. This is the card that turns width into combat lethality in one turn — hold it for the turn it kills.
card_roles.Skullclamp: One mana turns any 1/1 token into two cards, and the death feeds Blood Artist, Cruel Celebrant and Cordial Vampire on the way out. Clamp freely; you print bodies for a living.
card_roles.Night's Whisper: Two cards for two mana and two life — life this deck banks back by the handful. Cast it whenever you're not spending the turn on board.
card_roles.Pact of the Serpent: Name Vampire, target yourself, and draw a card per Vampire you control. Time it like Champion of Dusk: after the swarm, and mind your life total under your own drains.
card_roles.Welcoming Vampire: A card per turn for doing what you already do — putting small creatures onto the battlefield. Eminence alone triggers her every turn you cast a Vampire.
card_roles.Caretaker's Talent: Draws off your token entries — again, eminence triggers it for free — and the levels copy your best token and anthem the rest. Level up only when the mana is idle.
card_roles.Demonic Tutor: Best card in the deck at finding the missing kill half. Default target: the converter or doubler you lack — tutors take the turn-6 kill from 41.7% to 57.7%, and the infinite pieces don't pay that well.
card_roles.Vampiric Tutor: Same instruction as Demonic: fetch the missing converter or multiplier by default. It costs a turn of drawing the card, so fire it at an end step with a plan.
card_roles.Diabolic Intent: A tutor whose fee is a creature — which in this deck triggers your death drains and costs a token, not a card. The cheapest Demonic you'll ever cast.
card_roles.Teferi's Protection: The wipe insurance. Hold it for the turn you've committed the board or the turn their sweeper is on the stack — phasing out costs them the whole spell.
card_roles.Flawless Maneuver: Free with your commander out: the board survives the wrath and the drains collected on nothing. Keep one white source untapped as a bluff even when you don't have it.
card_roles.Akroma's Will: With Edgar on the field you take both modes: a protection spell and a kill spell in one card. Lifelink plus double strike on a wide board is usually just lethal.
card_roles.Boros Charm: Indestructible for the team at instant speed — or four to the face when four is what's left. The cheapest way to make a sweeper cost them a card for nothing.
card_roles.Deflecting Swat: Free with a commander you control: aim their removal at their own things, or retarget the drain aimed at your engine. Hold it; its whole value is that they can't see it.
card_roles.Swords to Plowshares: Best single-target answer in the format. Spend it on the card that beats you — the stax piece or the blocker that walls your swarm — not the scariest thing on the table.
card_roles.Path to Exile: Swords number two. The land they get matters less than the trigger-doubler or combo piece you exiled.
card_roles.Despark: Answers most things worth answering at instant speed — anything four mana or more, exiled. Save it for the permanent your creatures can't attack through.
card_roles.Anguished Unmaking: Exiles any nonland permanent for three life — life you bank back. Your cleanest answer to an enchantment or artifact engine.
card_roles.Generous Gift: Destroy anything — including a land locking you out — and the 3/3 they get is a body your drains eventually tax. Breadth is the point: this answers what nothing else in the 99 can.
card_roles.Stroke of Midnight: Gift's twin for nonlands, and the 1/1 they keep is a joke against your board. Your fifth and sixth true answers are what let you spend the first four early.
card_roles.Winds of Abandon: The one-sided reset: overloaded, every creature you don't control leaves and you keep the swarm. The basics they fetch matter far less than the combat that follows.
card_roles.Olivia's Wrath: Your sweeper, and it's one-sided by trade — non-Vampires get -X/-X for your Vampire count. Know your own five non-Vampire bodies eat it too; the death drains collect on the way down.
card_roles.Sol Ring: Two colourless a turn from turn one. It casts the generic half of everything; it never pays a coloured pip, so don't count it toward Bloodletter.
card_roles.Arcane Signet: Any of your three colours, every turn, forever. The rock you always keep in an opener light on lands.
card_roles.Talisman of Indulgence: Black or red on demand for a point of life — and black is the colour you're short. Tap it for B and take the ping happily.
card_roles.Bontu's Monument: Discounts every black creature and drains the table on every creature cast — a sixth converter that only counts your casts, not your tokens. It makes each eminence turn cheaper AND heavier.
card_roles.Herald's Horn: Discounts every Vampire and digs one off the top each upkeep. In a deck where most cards share a type, it's ramp and card advantage at once.
card_roles.Command Tower: All three colours, no questions. The best land in the deck.
card_roles.Cavern of Souls: Any colour for creature spells, uncounterable — but that mana pays for SPELLS only. It cannot activate Castle Locthwain, flip Bloodline Keeper, or pay any ability. Name Vampire and know the limit.
card_roles.Mana Confluence: Any colour for one life. In a deck that drains life back constantly, pay it without blinking.
card_roles.City of Brass: Confluence's twin — a point of life per tap for perfect fixing. Same instruction: the drains repay it.
card_roles.Reflecting Pool: Whatever your other lands make. Nearly always all three colours by turn 3.
card_roles.Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth: Every land you have taps for black — the colour carrying half your pips. It quietly fixes Bloodletter's triple-B all by itself.
card_roles.Nomad Outpost: All three colours, enters tapped. Play it on a turn you weren't spending anyway.
card_roles.Savai Triome: Three colours and a fetchable type — grab it with a fetch land early, cycle it never.
card_roles.Blood Crypt: Fetchable B/R dual. Pay the 2 life when you need it untapped; you'll get the life back.
card_roles.Godless Shrine: Fetchable W/B dual — the deck's two heaviest colours on one card.
card_roles.Sacred Foundry: Fetchable R/W dual. Third in the shock priority; fetch black first.
card_roles.Battlefield Forge: R or W untapped for a point of pain. Fine; the drains cover the tab.
card_roles.Caves of Koilos: W or B untapped for a point of pain — take it for black more often than not.
card_roles.Sulfurous Springs: B or R untapped for a point of pain. Same rule: black first.
card_roles.Silent Clearing: W/B pain land that becomes a card when the game goes long. Sacrifice it late before you flood.
card_roles.Blazemire Verge: B/R that's untapped whenever it matters in a deck this heavy on the pair.
card_roles.Bleachbone Verge: W/B, usually untapped, covering the two colours with the most pips.
card_roles.Concealed Courtyard: W/B untapped on the turns that decide aggro games — one through three.
card_roles.Haunted Ridge: B/R that's live from the mid-game on; sequence it after the slow lands.
card_roles.Shattered Sanctum: W/B, untapped with any other land in hand — which is nearly always.
card_roles.Sundown Pass: R/W with the same clause; play the basics and verges first.
card_roles.Luxury Suite: B/R, untapped in any multiplayer game — which is every game this deck plays.
card_roles.Spectator Seating: R/W with the same multiplayer clause. Untapped, effectively always.
card_roles.Vault of Champions: W/B with the same clause — a free Godless Shrine at a Commander table.
card_roles.Castle Locthwain: A draw engine on a land — expensive per card, cheapest when your hand is empty, which is exactly when an aggro deck needs it. It needs REAL black mana, not Cavern's.
card_roles.Minas Tirith: Untapped behind any of your thirteen legends, and it draws a card whenever you attack with two — you attack with seven.
card_roles.Takenuma, Abandoned Mire: A black source that channels a dead late draw into your best fallen creature. The only graveyard text in the 99, and it points at your own yard.
card_roles.Midgar, City of Mako // Reactor Raid: A black source or, late, a two-card refill priced at one token. Cast the sorcery when the board is wide and the land drop is spare.
card_roles.Ancient Tomb: Two mana per turn for two life — turn-3 Edgar money. The drains buy the life back.
card_roles.Bloodstained Mire: Fetches the shock you're missing. Black first, as always.
card_roles.Marsh Flats: Fetches Godless Shrine or a basic — grab black-producing land unless white is the hole.
card_roles.Prismatic Vista: Fetches either basic, untapped, at the cost of one life. Take the Swamp four times out of five.
card_roles.Plains: One of two basics — the Winds of Abandon and fetch target for white.
card_roles.Swamp: Four copies feeding the colour with half the deck's pips. When a fetch asks, this is usually the answer.

mulligan:
The model keeps 81.1% of first sevens on a two-to-five-land rule. Yours is tighter, because the measured failure is mana: 36 land copies, 15 entering tapped, 54 black pips across 38 cards, a turn-2 stall in 24.6% of games. Of 10,000 first sevens, 327 held no land, 1,477 one, 2,939 two, 2,972 three.

Keep three lands, or two lands and a rock (Sol Ring, Arcane Signet, Talisman of Indulgence), with a Vampire at one or two mana. A castable Vampire is drawn in 95.0% of games, and 96.4% of kept hands can act by turn 3. Viscera Seer turn one off a Swamp is the opener log 005 records. Weight the black source: on-curve black reads 0.855 with rocks and 0.785 on lands alone, against white 0.927.

Ship two lands with no rock. Log 002 is the case: one mulligan, a two-lander kept out of stubbornness, the game lost on mana. Even kept hands hit the turn-3 drop in 91.9% and the turn-4 drop in 80.9%, so a two-lander is betting on the top twice. Ship five or more lands with no Vampire under three mana; the eminence needs a spell, and extra cards drawn by turn 6 average 0.513.

Do not keep for a combo half. Bloodthirsty Conqueror and Sanguine Bond cost five, Bloodletter of Aclazotz four, Vito three, and none does anything before the board exists; the Conqueror pairing assembles in 7.8% of games, Bloodletter's in 4.1%. Keep for a curve, one payoff (Cordial Vampire, Blood Artist, Cruel Celebrant) and one draw piece (Welcoming Vampire, Night's Whisper, Skullclamp).

Edgar is not in the hand and does not need to be. The eminence works from the zone (stack 010), and he is cast by turn 6 in 60.3% of games. Plan his cast anyway: log 001 had him at eight mana for lack of attention.
upgrades:
Two numbers point at everything on this list: 27 and zero. Twenty-seven black sources against a Karsten target of 36 — 76.4% on-curve castability in the colour where every drain payoff lives — and zero answers to a graveyard, the one interaction class the 99 leaves open. Three of the ten move black mana; one, Soul-Guide Lantern, closes the graveyard for one colourless mana. Those four are plumbing, and plumbing is where a marginal dollar buys the most.

The rest are engine depth, and the headline is Exquisite Blood. The infinite currently rides on one body: Bloodthirsty Conqueror appears in 7.1% of opening sevens, and the line assembles unassisted in 4.8% of games. Add the enchantment and the pairings go from two to four — with Vito, Sanguine Bond and Conqueror all in the 99, every half suddenly has two partners — and both of its loops are checker-passed resolutions already on file. That's the cheapest consistency purchase available: not a new engine, a second copy of the one that's proven.

One famous card is absent on purpose. Rest in Peace would cover the graveyard gap for two mana, but under it creatures exile instead of dying — and a deck earning 62.6%-by-turn-6 conversion off entries and deaths cannot blank Blood Artist, Cruel Celebrant and Cordial Vampire to answer somebody else's yard. The Lantern does the job without the friendly fire. The 99 is locked for a piloting-practice stretch, so read the ten below as a watch list priced in advance: each entry names what it closes, what it unlocks, and what it would naturally replace.
mana_base:
Thirty-seven land copies across 34 entries, and one ratio runs the show: black is 51.3% of the pip demand on 42.9% of the sources. Twenty-seven black sources — 24 lands plus three rocks — against a Karsten double-pip target of 36, for 76.4% on-curve. Red is the mirror image, 14.5% of the pips on 25% of the sources.

That 36 is a yardstick, not a destination — no 37-land aggro list reaches it. Rocks included, the honest reading is white 89.5%, red 83.1%, black 76.4%. That last number is what a triple-B Bloodletter and a double-black quorum cost in a deck that refuses to slow down for them. The white and red halves cast themselves; the black cards are the casts you plan.

Fifteen of 37 lands can enter tapped, 41% against a one-in-three budget — but only three always do. The other twelve want a multiplayer table, a second land in hand, a legend on board, and this deck supplies all three. The goldfish doesn't flinch: 91.9% hit the turn-3 land drop, 5.3 mana available by turn six, 80.8% of sevens kept.

The rocks split three ways. Sol Ring is generic and never pays a pip; Arcane Signet and Patchwork Banner cover all three colours; Talisman of Indulgence adds the black the deck is short, at a life a tap the drains repay. Herald's Horn and Bontu's Monument are discounts rather than sources, and the simulation doesn't model them — so every figure above is conservative by roughly their contribution.

Two bits of fine print. Cavern of Souls makes coloured mana for creature spells only: it accelerates the tribe and powers none of the machinery, not Castle Locthwain's draw and not Bloodline Keeper's flip. And City of Brass plus Mana Confluence charge a life a tap for perfect fixing — in a deck that banked 7 life on one verified attack (stack 003), that is the cheapest fixing money can buy.
threat_assessment:
You are the archenemy from the first Vampire cast. Log 001: five bodies by turn three off three mana, and the table's answers came at you first. That is the price of the plan.

The wipe. The pod runs heavy creature removal and heavy wipes (log 002). With Blood Artist, Cruel Celebrant, Cordial Vampire, Elenda or Crossway Troublemakers out, a wipe pays you: eleven deaths, 11 off every opponent, in log 002. Without a payoff out, redeploy worst-first and hold the second Vampire. Of the five protection spells, Flawless Maneuver, Boros Charm and Akroma's Will's second mode answer destroy; only Teferi's Protection answers exile, bounce or -X/-X. Only Teferi's Protection and Boros Charm reach the noncreature pieces: Anointed Procession, Sanguine Bond, Blade of the Bloodchief, Elspeth. Flawless Maneuver and Deflecting Swat are free only while Edgar is on the battlefield, which is turn 6 or earlier in 60.3% of games. Before that, interaction is castable on 26.9% of turn-6 boards while it is in hand on 88.3%: the mana goes on Vampires. Decide each turn whether the next Vampire beats the held spell.

Open mana. A seat passing with four or more untapped and nothing on board is holding a sweeper or a counter. Stated assumption. Against blue, Champion of Dusk and Bloodthirsty Conqueror are what got countered (log 001). Cast the refuel when the blue seat is tapped, or behind a bait spell.

Noncreature removal. Ryan's recurring artifact and enchantment removal took Anointed Procession the turn after it landed (log 002). Creature removal aimed at tokens fed the draw in log 004; removal aimed at the converters starved it in 002. What a seat's removal is pointed at decides whether it runs your engine or ends it.

The trigger racer. Purphoros pinged the table out in log 005 while Elspeth was exposed. Forge on v1.1.0, seated with purphoros-pingers: 4 of 38 decided games; the pinger won 19. Two cards exile an indestructible noncreature permanent: Despark (mana value 4 or more) and Anguished Unmaking. Stroke of Midnight destroys and does not. Teferi's Protection buys one turn cycle. Once a planeswalker is online, keep blockers up and protect the engine before pushing tempo. That is the 2026-09-15 lesson.

Your tells. Bloodthirsty Conqueror, Vito, Sanguine Bond and Bloodletter of Aclazotz read as a combo whether or not you fire one. Sequence them after the removal is spent. Close when the close is there: both v1.1.0 games ended with lethal in sight (004, 005).
matchups:
Sweeper control. Hold Cruel Celebrant or Blood Artist for the board, not the turn-one curve: a wipe with a payoff out is your drain (log 002). Deploy in waves. The eminence rebuilds from a zone no sweeper touches; log 001 rebuilt through three wipes. Hold Teferi's Protection for a board that matters; two tokens was not one (002). The card that flips it is Elenda: she grows on every death, theirs included, and dies into lifelink Vampires under the doublers, so a wipe with her out leaves you a board. The count needs a stack scenario.

Counter-heavy blue. Two counters decided log 001: Champion of Dusk and Bloodthirsty Conqueror. Deploy the cheap Vampires into open blue mana; they are eminence triggers and not worth a counter. Hold the refuel until the seat taps down, or lead with a Vampire of similar size as bait. Vampiric Tutor is an instant and reveals nothing; cast it at their end step.

Stax and taxes. 27 of 64 nonland entries cost two or less, and the thirteen Vampires among them are the triggers, so a tax halves the fodder as well as the casts. You are the beatdown against a lock; race it. Outs: Anguished Unmaking, Despark, Stroke of Midnight. Nothing in the 99 answers a land, and interaction breadth reads three classes (artifact, creature, enchantment). Six outlets need no mana and no tap, the one part of the engine a tax cannot touch.

Aggro. Eight bodies carry printed lifelink, and Elenda, Legion's Landing, Mavren Fein and Charismatic Conqueror make lifelink tokens. Block with a deathtouch lifelinker: Gifted Aetherborn, Vampire of the Dire Moon, Nighthawk Scavenger. Pay life early on Champion of Dusk, Night's Whisper and Crossway Troublemakers, and stop paying the turn a burn seat has you in range. Vito or Sanguine Bond flips it: every point gained is a point drained.

Combo. No counterspell; Deflecting Swat retargets a spell or ability and is free with Edgar out. The clock is the lever. Log 004 lost to a tutored infinite with lethal on board, so against a combo seat the last profitable moment to commit is now. Bloodletter with Sanctum Seeker (stack 003) is the compressed close: 14 per seat on attack declaration.

ETB trigger racer (Purphoros). The predator on record: 0-1 at the table (005), 4/38 decided in Forge on v1.1.0. Blockers do not help. Despark or Anguished Unmaking on the enchantment does, and Teferi's Protection buys a turn. Stop feeding it entries you do not need. Attack-first versus hold is unsettled.
editors_letter:
The card that runs this deck is the one card you will never draw.

Edgar Markov mints a Vampire every time you cast a Vampire, and he does it from the command zone — so the engine is switched on in game one, on turn one, whether or not you get around to paying six mana for the body. Everything else in the 99 feeds that fact: a curve made almost entirely of one- and two-mana creatures, doublers that turn one token into four, and payoffs that bill all three opponents for the privilege of a body existing.

Coach Brightside opens the log with what follows from that, and it sounds like a misplay out loud. The Counselor agrees with him on the rule and then takes about a third of the claim away, which is the best exchange in the issue. Ledger has the rates for the two lines nobody should plan around.

You will have a good time here if you want your whole turn to be a two-mana creature and you want that to be enough — if you like watching three life totals move at once off a card nobody bothered to read. You will not, if you are waiting for a big turn. This deck does not have one. It has a great many small ones, and it wants all of them.

One warning, from the Counselor's file: the kill that is on the record is exactly lethal. Not comfortably. Exactly.

pilots_log.text: Turn six, somebody points removal at Edgar Markov and the whole table relaxes. The removal that beats this deck is the removal that does not kill your commander. Kill Edgar, exile him, catch him in a wrath — he goes to the command zone, and the command zone is where he was already working from. The card you actually have to answer is the one that leaves him standing there doing nothing.

The rule is with the Coach. The scope of it is not, quite.

The load-bearing half is on the record. Stack 002 resolves eminence with Edgar in the command zone and rechecks the intervening 'if' on resolution, which is what CR 113.6b buys: 'an ability that states which zones it functions in functions only from those zones.' Eminence names the command zone. And CR 903.9a is why destruction and exile are a wash — a commander on its way to a graveyard or to exile may be put into the command zone instead, and that is a zone the ability already works in.

What the Coach did not say, and I will: the effects he is pointing at appear in no passing stack. An aura that leaves him on the battlefield with his abilities stripped, or an effect that takes control of him, works because he never changes zones, so 903.9a never fires and there is nothing to recur. That is printed text plus a rule, applied correctly, and no checker has run it.

And the arrow this engine cannot do without — his mint feeding the doublers — is drawn dashed in the deck's own engine file, because none of the three scenarios that resolve his trigger names him on its board. That is a bookkeeping absence rather than a rules one. It is still an absence.

The holding: he is right that you cannot switch this engine off by removing this card. On the things that can switch it off, he is reading rather than quoting.

What the body is worth, since the Coach is offering it up. Ten thousand seeded runs: Edgar Markov is cast by turn six in 52.1% of them, mean turn 6.614, median six. In 1,608 of the 10,000 he is not cast by turn ten at all.

Bodies on the board while that is going on: 2.921 at turn four, 4.221 at turn six, 5.466 at turn eight. Mean available mana at turn six is 5.348, which is one short of his cost.

The rates the engine runs on do not wait for him. A converter is drawn in 73.5% of runs, 62.6% by turn six, mean turn 2.832. A multiplier in 78.9%, 68.2% by turn six. Both halves together, 57.4% and 41.7%.

Taken, and here is what I do with it at the table.

Stop treating the six-drop as the thing you are building toward. He is a late bonus and your engine has been running since your first Vampire.

Then point your answers where the Counselor just pointed. You have eight of them — Despark, Anguished Unmaking, Generous Gift, Stroke of Midnight, Path to Exile, Swords to Plowshares, Winds of Abandon, Olivia's Wrath — and the temptation every time is to spend one on the scariest permanent in the pod. Don't. Spend it on the enchantment sitting on your own commander. That is the one that turned you off. The rest of them only made you unhappy.

And when he does land he is not a token engine, which is the half the Coach skipped past.

Stack 003 is the one passing stack whose board actually holds him, and it resolves his attack trigger: seven attackers, a +1/+1 counter on each. It also prices the drain beside it, and this part is worth memorising. Seven Vampires attack, so Sanctum Seeker triggers seven separate times, and with Bloodletter of Aclazotz out each of those triggers takes two from each opponent instead of one, because it is your turn. Your own life gain is not doubled — Bloodletter replaces an opponent's loss and nothing else. The opponent at 14 reaches exactly zero on the seventh trigger and loses to state-based actions before a blocker is declared. You finish that combat at 33 without one.

Fourteen a seat, at declare-attackers. It is a combat kill in which no combat occurs.

The price of that sentence is one card, and here is the price.

Bloodletter of Aclazotz is a 1-of. Its declared component — Bloodletter plus a drain source — assembles in 5.2% of runs, 3.1% by turn six, mean turn 5.377. With the three tutors modelled, 24.6%.

Beside it, the two-card loop through Bloodthirsty Conqueror: 4.8% assembled, 2.9% by turn six, 24.3% assisted. Those are the two lowest figures in the declaration and they are the same size as each other.

The go-wide kill, for comparison: 57.4% assembled, 41.7% by turn six, 57.7% by turn six with tutors, mean turn 4.188.

Which is my whole point, and it is the thing pilots get backwards on this deck. The two lines you would tell a story about afterwards are the two you will hardly ever draw.

So go and look at the one board in this file where a whole pod dies. Bloodletter is not on it. The Conqueror is not on it. There is no combat step on it. You cast a two-mana Vampire. That is the turn.

Correct, and I will put the arithmetic on it — with one disclosure first, since the Coach raised the loop. Stacks 004 and 006 each begin from three life gained 'from some source.' Everything above that seed is proved: 13 Vito resolutions, no mana, no cards, a dead table. Where the first three life come from is a claim nothing in this file verifies.

Now stack 009, which needs none of it. Your board is Purphoros, God of the Forge, Impact Tremors, Warleader's Call, Anointed Procession, five lands and no creatures at all. You cast Cordial Vampire for {B}{B}. Eminence mints one token, Anointed Procession makes it two, and both enter as a single event containing two occurrences — CR 603.2c: an ability 'can trigger repeatedly if one event contains multiple occurrences.' Then the Vampire itself enters. Three entries, three payoffs, nine triggers. Purphoros twice per entry and the other two once each: twelve damage to each opponent.

Three seats at twelve. Exactly lethal, zero margin — one trigger fewer and all three of them are alive at one or two. And Purphoros is not a creature on that board; devotion to red is three. That costs you a body and does nothing whatever to the trigger.

Two figures to keep attached to that.

The pod total on stack 009 is 36 and the per-seat figure is 12. They are not interchangeable, and only the second one describes a table.

And every checked board starts low. Stack 009 opens at 12 a seat; stack 003 at 21 and 14; stack 007 at 15 and 9; stack 008 at 24 and 10. None of them opens at 40. How many two-mana casts it takes to move one untouched seat from 40 to 0 with a single doubler is written in the engine file as an open question, and it has no number attached.

What has numbers: 4.221 bodies by turn six, a converter at mean turn 2.832, a multiplier at mean turn 2.703.

All right, then here is the version I actually use — and somebody stop me if the count is off.

Seven cards here turn a body into other people's life total: Purphoros, Impact Tremors, Warleader's Call, Witty Roastmaster, Corpse Knight, Blood Artist, Cruel Celebrant. Seven. Which means the wrath everybody is holding pays me too — all seven bill the table again on the way down. And Bontu's Monument is making the little Vampires cheaper the whole time I am doing it.

Two corrections, Coach, and each one changes how you sequence a turn.

One. Five of your seven trigger on a creature ENTERING — Purphoros, Impact Tremors, Warleader's Call and Witty Roastmaster deal damage, Corpse Knight causes life loss. Two trigger on a creature DYING: Blood Artist and Cruel Celebrant. Under a wrath you collect on two of the seven, not seven. And of those two, only Cruel Celebrant reaches each opponent — Blood Artist drains one target player, your choice, one seat. That is printed text and not a stack, and what a resolved sweeper actually pays you is filed in this deck's engine as a question nobody has run.

Two. Bontu's Monument reduces the generic part of a cost, and CR 601.2f is plain that a generic reduction cannot pay a coloured pip. Cordial Vampire costs {B}{B}. It has no generic part, so the Monument does nothing for it — and nine of the twenty-one black creature spells in this deck are the same shape. They are precisely the cheap bodies you want to be casting every turn.

Plainly: for those nine, Bontu's Monument is a drain trigger, not a discount.

The colour underneath both of those.

Black is 39 of this deck's 76 coloured pips, spread over 29 cards. It has 24 land sources, 27 counting the rocks, against a 36-source yardstick for casting on curve at the 90% standard. On-curve black comes out at 69.4% on lands alone and 76.4% with the rocks.

White: 26 pips, 21 sources, 89.5%. Red: 11 pips, 17 sources, 83.1%.

Fifteen of the 37 lands enter tapped. Land-drop hit rate is 91.9% at turn three and 58.9% at turn six. First seven kept 80.8% of the time, mean mulligans 0.227.

The drains are the black cards.

So play it like this.

Turn one, turn two, turn three: cast the cheapest Vampire in your hand every single turn, including the one that looks like it does nothing. The token is the point, and every token is a bill sent to three people at once.

Lead on the untapped black source. The Counselor just told you which nine casts cannot be discounted, and a land entering tapped is exactly how you miss one of them.

Do not wait on the six-drop. Do not build toward the loop. Find a payoff, find a doubler, then cast a two-mana creature into a table that stopped counting your board three turns ago because it is all 1/1s.

And when you get there, count twelve a seat — not thirty-six across the table. She said zero margin and she meant it. One trigger short and all three of them are still there, still alive, and it is about to be their turn.
